question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man was sent to the nephrology service by his primary internist after routine laboratory testing showed a rise in serum creatinine from 2.6 mg/dL six months ago to 3.1 mg/dL last week, with an accompanying estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24 mL/min/1.73 m². He reports gradually worsening early-morning fatigue and new nocturnal muscle cramps in the calves, but no dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, or ankle swelling. Blood pressure at home averages 136/78 mm Hg on lisinopril 20 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg nightly. Ten years ago he was told that long-standing hypertension and microvascular ischemia of the kidneys were responsible for a slowly progressive decline in renal function; he has never required dialysis, but recent discussions have centered on possible pre-transplant evaluation. He strongly denies any episodes of prolonged chest pressure, emergent cardiac catheterization, hospital admissions for pump failure, or ever being told he sustained a heart attack, and he walks two flights of stairs without substernal discomfort or undue shortness of breath. Intermittent brief neurologic events occurred two summers ago: three episodes of transient right-hand numbness accompanied by word-finding difficulty, each resolving within 15 minutes without residual weakness. Work-up at that time, including non-contrast head CT and carotid duplex ultrasound, revealed no acute infarct or hemodynamically significant plaque, yet aspirin 81 mg daily and high-intensity statin therapy were initiated and no further spells have occurred. He denies sudden unilateral paralysis, visual field loss, or facial droop at any other time. Five years earlier he was hospitalized for hematemesis and melena; upper endoscopy demonstrated a 2-cm clean-based posterior duodenal ulcer with no visible vessel. He completed an eradication course for Helicobacter pylori, has remained on omeprazole 40 mg twice daily, and undergoes annual hemoglobin checks that have stayed above 13 g/dL. Since his twenties, liver chemistry panels have shown alanine aminotransferase values in the low 60s U/L and aspartate aminotransferase in the mid-40s U/L; abdominal ultrasound last winter again described mild diffuse hepatic steatosis without nodularity, ascites, or portal vein dilatation, and he has never manifested jaundice, easy bruising, encephalopathy, or variceal bleeding. Fasting glucose readings have persistently ranged between 88 and 104 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c obtained last month measured 5.7 %, so he continues to rely on dietary carbohydrate restriction alone. He is a lifelong nonsmoker, drinks two bottles of beer on weekends, and has never used illicit substances. He has never been diagnosed with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis and has never required maintenance inhaler therapy. He reports no history of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma, vasculitis, or other connective tissue disorders. He has not experienced rest pain, non-healing lower-extremity ulcers, or required vascular surgery for limb ischemia. He has never been diagnosed with any form of cancer, including solid organ or lymphoid malignancy, and his prior screening HIV testing has been negative. Family history is notable for a father who required coronary bypass at 72 and a sister who developed an ischemic stroke in her sixties; there is no familial kidney disease. Current medications include lisinopril, amlodipine, aspirin, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, omeprazole, cholecalciferol, and an over-the-counter magnesium supplement for cramps; he takes no nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories or nephrotoxic herbal preparations. Review of systems elicits no cough, wheeze, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, claudication, abdominal pain, hematochezia, dark urine, pruritus, photosensitive rash, or joint swelling. On arrival he appears well nourished, alert, and in no acute distress. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 138/80 mm Hg in the right arm seated, heart rate 74 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air, body mass index 28 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsation is 6 cm H₂O, carotid upstroke brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced. Cardiac examination reveals a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout. Abdomen is soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge is palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, smooth, and mildly tender to percussion, and no splenomegaly or shifting dullness is detected. Extremities show no edema; radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally, and there is no femoral bruit. Neurologic evaluation demonstrates fluent speech, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength throughout, normal tone, symmetric reflexes, intact vibration and light-touch sensation, and steady tandem gait. Skin inspection reveals well-healed scars from prior intravenous line placements but no telangiectasias, palmar erythema, or spider angiomas. Laboratory studies drawn this morning reveal sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 5.0 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 54 mg/dL, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, calcium 8.4 mg/dL, phosphorus 4.9 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 102 U/L, AST 48 U/L, ALT 61 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, international normalized ratio 1.1, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.2 × 10⁹/L, and platelets 248 × 10⁹/L. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein, no blood, and few granular casts; spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.6 g/g. Electrocardiogram obtained in clinic demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 72 beats/min, axis within normal limits, no pathologic Q waves, and unchanged T-wave morphology. A recent transthoracic echocardiogram available in the electronic record lists left ventricular ejection fraction 58 %, no regional wall-motion abnormality, and normal valvular function. Duplex imaging of the renal arteries six months ago revealed mild intimal thickening without flow-limiting stenosis. The patient seeks guidance on slowing kidney decline, assessing candidacy for future renal replacement therapy, and ensuring control of associated comorbid conditions identified in prior hospitalizations.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index adds age points to weighted comorbidity points.
- Age 59 (50–59 years) → 1.
- Moderate to severe renal disease: advanced CKD with admission creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, above the 3 mg/dL threshold → 2. Dialysis is not required to meet this criterion.
- Cerebrovascular disease: transient focal sensory and language deficits are consistent with prior TIAs, which count even without an imaging-confirmed infarct → 1.
- Peptic ulcer disease: prior bleeding duodenal ulcer documented by endoscopy → 1.
- Mild chronic liver disease: persistent hepatic steatosis and transaminase elevation without portal hypertension → 1.
- Other CCI conditions → 0. Hypertension and prediabetes do not add points.
Total: 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6.
Final answer: 6
